segments.t: While walking through the dining room, Chef Barinov's daughter Katya spots her childhood friend Lilya. The two women have competed fiercely since kindergarten, so when Lilya introduces her wealthy husband, Katya invents a fiancé on the spot. Let's listen to their rivalry in Russian.
Let's examine Katya and Lilya's competitive reunion line by line.
'Hello, this is my friend Katya.' Lilya greets Katya casually and introduces her using a demonstrative pronoun and a feminine noun for a female friend.
'We went to kindergarten together.' A multidirectional past-tense verb of motion expresses repeated round-trip attendance in childhood.
'We always argued since childhood.' Katya recalls their lifelong rivalry with a frequency adverb and a plural imperfective past verb.
'They accepted me into the university back then.' An impersonal third-person plural past verb with an accusative pronoun means being admitted to school.
'And I went to France.' Katya counters using a contrastive conjunction and an accusative destination phrase for France.
'Katya, this is my husband Ernest.' Lilya proudly presents her spouse with a masculine possessive determiner.
'Hello, it is very nice to meet you.' The standard polite greeting phrase pairs naturally with a reflexive perfective infinitive.
'Well, and did you get married?' For a woman, Russian uses a specific verbal idiom literally meaning to step out behind a husband.
'No, but I will definitely get married soon.' Katya uses the first-person singular perfective future verb with a temporal adverb meaning soon.
'Our wedding is in a month.' A temporal preposition plus an accusative noun marks how soon the wedding will happen.
'Then let's have dinner together tomorrow evening!' The first-person plural perfective future verb functions as an enthusiastic dinner invitation.
'I do not know, he is very busy.' Katya tries to stall with a masculine singular short-form predicate adjective meaning busy.
'Great, what time are we meeting tomorrow?' An interrogative time phrase asks for the exact hour of their scheduled meeting. Let's listen to their dining room conversation again without interruption.
Katya's pride traps her into promising to bring her non-existent fiancé to dinner the very next evening. Listen for the feminine phrase for getting married in Russian. See you in the next scene.
